name: Trino
summary: A distributed SQL engine that queries data where it lives, from Iceberg tables on S3 to a live PostgreSQL database, in one query.
intro: A Trino cluster has one coordinator and many workers. The coordinator parses and plans each query and splits it into stages. Workers pull data through connectors and stream intermediate results to each other in memory, stage to stage, rather than writing them to disk in between. That makes Trino good at interactive queries that finish in seconds over large tables.

Each catalog is a connector: Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hive and Hudi for lake tables, plus PostgreSQL, MySQL, Kafka, MongoDB, BigQuery and many more, so one query can join an Iceberg table with a live PostgreSQL table. Presto’s creators built the original at Facebook in 2012, left in 2018 to continue it as PrestoSQL, and renamed it Trino in December 2020. Amazon Athena’s current engine is built from Trino.
strengths: Federation: join lake tables with operational databases without copying either
Reads and writes Iceberg and Delta Lake tables, including UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE
ANSI SQL and more than 35 connectors
Apache 2.0, with managed versions such as Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR and Starburst
limits: A long-running cluster to size and operate; by default a query fails if a node runs out of resources, unless you turn on fault-tolerant execution
No storage of its own, so speed depends on file layout, partitioning and table statistics
Hudi support is read-only, and merge-on-read tables are seen only as of their last compaction
Iceberg v3 support is experimental, without row-level updates or deletes on v3 tables

story: By 2012, Facebook’s data warehouse held more than 300 petabytes in Hadoop, and analysts queried it through Hive. Hive turned each SQL query into MapReduce jobs, which were designed for large-scale, reliable computation and optimised for overall throughput, with every stage writing to disk. At that scale Facebook needed an interactive system optimised for low query latency.

In fall 2012, Martin Traverso, Dain Sundstrom, David Phillips and Eric Hwang, on Facebook’s Data Infrastructure team, set out to build that system, and they wanted it open source from the start. Presto went into production in early 2013 and was open-sourced that November. By then it ran more than 30,000 queries a day, scanning a petabyte, and Facebook reported it was 10x better than Hive/MapReduce in CPU efficiency and latency. Uber, Netflix and Airbnb adopted it, and Amazon based its Athena service on it.

In 2018 Facebook wanted tighter control of the project, so Traverso, Sundstrom and Phillips left and in January 2019 started the Presto Software Foundation to continue their version, PrestoSQL. Facebook set up a rival Presto Foundation under the Linux Foundation and applied for the Presto trademark, so in December 2020 the creators renamed their fork Trino.

choices.choice: Pipelined, in-memory execution instead of MapReduce
choices.why: MapReduce wrote every stage’s output to disk before the next could start. Presto streams data from one stage to the next as it becomes available, which is what made ad-hoc queries interactive.

choices.choice: A connector API instead of its own storage
choices.why: Facebook’s data lived in HDFS, HBase and custom systems such as the News Feed backend. A simple storage abstraction let one engine query all of them, and is why Trino can join an Iceberg table with PostgreSQL today.

choices.choice: Java, with query plans compiled to bytecode
choices.why: Java was fast to develop in and fit Facebook’s Hadoop infrastructure. Generating JVM bytecode for each query plan lets the JIT compiler optimise the hot loops.

choices.choice: Fault tolerance added later, as an option
choices.why: Skipping disk checkpoints made queries fast but meant one failed node killed the whole query. Project Tardigrade (2022) added optional retries with spooled data so long ETL jobs can survive failures.

timeline.text: Presto started at Facebook in the fall
In production early in the year; open-sourced in November
Amazon Athena launches, built on Presto
Creators leave Facebook and form the Presto Software Foundation (PrestoSQL)
Fault-tolerant execution (Project Tardigrade); Athena engine 3 adopts Trino
